name: gnu-go
why: A full Go engine from the GNU project, an old-school board game opponent with a deep history and a genuinely rich game.

brief.what_it_is: GNU Go is a free program that plays the game of Go. You run it as a computer opponent, and it is also used as a playing engine by Go clients and servers. The homepage says it has played thousands of games on the NNGS Go server and plays regularly on the Legend Go Server in Taiwan and the WING server in Japan, and that volunteers run GNU Go clients on KGS. The documentation describes a Go Text Protocol (GTP) mode, an ASCII interface, and clients such as CGoban and an Emacs mode, so the inputs and outputs are Go moves and positions, most likely via a terminal or GTP connection. I did not see the exact input and output formats in the pages I read.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents GNU Go as a free, non-commercial Go program, and says it has established itself as the leading non-commercial Go program in recent tournaments it has entered.
brief.how_it_works: The documentation table of contents describes an engine built from tactical reading, pattern databases, influence functions, eye-space analysis, and a Monte Carlo component, with move generators that propose moves and a valuation step that scores them. I only saw section headings, not the explanations, so treat these as the documented structure rather than a verified description of the algorithm.
brief.install_notes: The homepage says GNU Go 3.8 (released February 19, 2009) is portable and known to work on GNU/Linux, Windows and Mac OS/X. The documentation table of contents lists installation sections for GNU/Linux and Unix, configure options (such as a RAM cache and default level), several Windows build routes (older Visual Studio, Visual Studio project files, Nmake, MinGW, MSYS, Cygwin), and a Macintosh section. I did not open those pages, so I have no specific commands or prerequisites from them.
brief.standout: It is one of the older free Go engines, with a long public history and a large documented internal design, covering pattern matching, tactical reading, and influence, plus regular play on public Go servers. The docs also include a full texinfo manual converted to HTML, which is unusual for a game engine of this age.
brief.status: Quiet. The homepage names GNU Go 3.8, released February 19, 2009, as the latest stable version, and the page's revision stamp is dated 2019. I found no newer release mentioned in the pages I read, so the last stable release I can confirm is from 2009. I did not check the release history or commit activity.
brief.caveats: The latest stable release I could confirm is 3.8 from 2009, so the code is old. The homepage says the software is portable across GNU/Linux, Windows and Mac OS/X, but the Windows build paths in the documentation are numerous and suggest some setup effort. The homepage lists no licence, but the documentation table of contents includes the GNU General Public License and the GNU Free Documentation License. I did not see whether a Homebrew formula carries extra caveats.
quotes: GNU Go is a free program that plays the game of Go.
GNU Go has established itself as the leading non-commercial go program in the recent tournaments that it has taken part in.
GNU Go 3.8, released February 19, 2009, is the latest stable version.
